evals.name: modern-language-refactor
evals.expected_output: A concise modernization that uses guard preconditions, typed throws for the single validation error domain, switch expressions for conditional return, collection APIs such as count(where:), and explains why each change is appropriate.
assertions: Uses `throws(ValidationError)` or explicitly recommends typed throws for the single validation error domain.
Rewrites `iconName(priority:)` with a `switch` expression or equivalent single-expression return without a mutable temporary variable.
Uses `count(where:)` rather than a manual loop for counting urgent tags.
Keeps the answer focused on Swift language idioms and does not expand into SwiftUI, concurrency, or lint configuration.

evals.name: swift63-interop-attributes
evals.prompt:
Correct this Swift 6.3 interoperability/performance note for a team wiki. The draft says: `@c func export(_ bytes: UnsafeBufferPointer<UInt8>) -> Int32` is valid C export syntax, `@specialize` is the official function-specialization attribute, `@inline(always)` is just a hint, and module selectors are written `ModuleName.symbol`.

Give a corrected note with minimal Swift examples.
evals.expected_output: A source-grounded correction that uses a C-compatible @c signature, names @specialized as the official explicit-specialization attribute, treats @inline(always) as a guaranteed inlining request that can fail when impossible, and uses ModuleName::symbol module selectors.
assertions: Rejects `UnsafeBufferPointer<UInt8>` in an `@c` exported function signature because it is a Swift struct, not a C-representable parameter.
Shows an `@c` example using C-compatible pointer and scalar types, optionally with a custom C symbol name.
States that Swift 6.3 `@inline(always)` guarantees inlining for direct calls and can produce an error when inlining is impossible.

evals.name: adjacent-domain-routing
evals.prompt: I have three cleanup requests in Scholium's macOS package: build full Codable wire models with snake_case keys and date decoding, design locale-sensitive date/list formatting for researchers in several regions, and decide whether a reusable Swift helper should use `some`, `any`, or `Never`. Which parts should the Swift language skill own, and how should it route the adjacent work when no dedicated Codable or localization skill is installed? Include only minimal examples.
evals.expected_output: A boundary-aware answer that keeps swift-language focused on core type-system features such as some/any/Never, identifies full Codable model design and locale-sensitive formatting as adjacent work, and points to the live API contract, project guidance, tests, or official framework documentation without inventing unavailable sibling skills.
assertions: Says swift-language owns the core type-system/language decision around `some`, `any`, and `Never`.
Correctly explains that `Never` is uninhabited/bottom-type-like in expression contexts but does not implicitly conform to arbitrary protocols.
Identifies full Codable API model design, key strategies, and date decoding as an adjacent domain and points to the live API contract or official Codable documentation.
Identifies locale-sensitive display work as an adjacent domain and points to project localization guidance, locale-matrix tests, or official FormatStyle documentation.
Does not claim an unavailable sibling skill is installed.
Does not provide a full Codable model suite or full formatting/localization implementation.
